strengths: Genuinely interesting theoretical mechanism (continuity via max over equicontinuous families) that offers a fresh perspective on a well-known impossibility result in canonicalization.
Concrete, creative instantiations in spectral GNNs and point-cloud networks with an anisotropic interpretation that is intuitive and well-motivated.

Consistent empirical improvements over a fairly comprehensive set of baselines (equivariant architectures, augmentation, and other canonicalization methods) across multiple domains: toy synthetic task, TUDataset, OGB molecular/protein benchmarks, and ModelNet40 point clouds, including an out-of-distribution rotation generalization test.
Reasonably extensive supplementary material with proofs, additional continuity examples, and ablations examining the sampling-vs-optimization trade-off and node- vs graph-level constructions.
weaknesses: The exact prior-maximization operation requires solving an optimization over the transformation group (SO(3), O(M_k), etc.) separately for each of the D classes at every forward pass (training and inference), which is computationally expensive and scales linearly with the number of classes; this is problematic for datasets with many classes/tasks (e.g., ogbg-molpcba has 128 tasks). No wall-clock runtime or memory comparison against baselines is reported, despite this being central to practical feasibility.

The theoretical continuity/universal-approximation guarantees rely on solving the max exactly; in practice the paper uses an approximate "sample-and-refine" heuristic (random Haar sampling + a few unrolled-but-not-backpropagated gradient steps). This approximate procedure is not shown to preserve the continuity guarantees that motivate the whole framework, creating a gap between the elegant theory and the deployed algorithm that is not adequately analyzed (e.g., no bound on how approximation error affects continuity/stability in practice).

The framework as developed is restricted to classification (one-vs-rest formulation with per-class confidence maximization); the authors explicitly acknowledge regression is unaddressed, which significantly narrows applicability relative to general equivariant learning (e.g., force field prediction, many geometric regression tasks).

Some empirical results lack full transparency: Table 3 (ModelNet40) reports no standard deviations/error bars, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains over VN-DGCNN/CN-DGCNN (e.g., 91.7 vs 90.2/90.0) are statistically meaningful; similarly Table 7 (z/SO(3)) has no variance reported.

The illustrative toy example (grid signal orientation task) is explicitly constructed to require per-orientation anisotropic sensitivity, which mechanically favors the proposed method and makes other baselines trivially fail at chance level; while this cleanly demonstrates the concept, it offers limited insight into performance on more realistic anisotropic-sensitivity scenarios.

Missing comparisons to some strong, more specialized equivariant architectures (e.g., SE(3)-Transformers, Tensor Field Networks, EGNN) for point clouds/molecules, and to more recent graph transformer/positional-encoding methods for TUDataset, limiting the completeness of the empirical positioning.

The per-class canonicalization approach (each class gets its own learned optimal transformation) is a fairly strong and somewhat unusual inductive bias/oracle-like mechanism that essentially grants the model D independent "views" of the same input; the paper does not fully discuss whether this could lead to overfitting or memorization-like behavior in cases with many classes or small per-class training data, nor does it compare against a natural ablation where a single shared (non-class-specific) canonicalization is learned.

strengths: Addresses a well-known and theoretically significant problem (discontinuity of canonicalization maps, as highlighted by Dym et al. 2024) with a conceptually appealing fix: making the canonicalization depend jointly on the input and the (trained) network via prior maximization.

Provides a reasonably complete theoretical package: definitions of adaptive canonicalization, proofs of equicontinuity/continuity (Thm 8, 9), symmetry preservation (Thm 12), and universal approximation (Thm 6, 13), situated within a general locally-compact-Hausdorff/galaxy formalism that covers graphs and point clouds.

Broad empirical validation across several domains (toy orientation task, TUDataset, large-scale OGB molecular/protein benchmarks, ModelNet40 point clouds) with consistent, often sizable improvements over canonicalization, augmentation, and equivariant baselines.

Includes informative ablations, e.g., sampling-based vs. optimization-based (sample-and-refine) implementation trade-offs, node- vs. graph-level spectral construction, and an out-of-distribution SO(3) generalization test for point clouds.
weaknesses: Fundamental scalability concern: prior maximization requires solving D separate optimization (search/refinement over rotations or orthogonal groups) problems per input, one per class, at both training and inference time. This is acknowledged as a limitation but never empirically analyzed (no runtime/memory numbers reported), and it is especially concerning for datasets with many classes such as ogbg-molpcba (128 classes), where 128 per-sample rotation/orthogonal-group optimizations seem highly impractical; the paper reports strong accuracy there without any discussion of the corresponding computational overhead.

There is a substantial theory-practice gap: the continuity and universal approximation guarantees are proven for an idealized exact maximizer over a compact group, but the actual implementation uses a heuristic 'sample a few random candidates + a few local gradient steps' procedure (not differentiated through) with loosely specified hyperparameters ('a few additional GD steps', unspecified sample budget in main experiments). It is unclear whether the practical estimator retains the claimed continuity/UAT properties, since an approximate, possibly non-global maximizer could reintroduce discontinuities the paper claims to solve.

Reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence in the empirical claims: Table 1 and Table 2 report means with standard deviations, but Table 3 (ModelNet40) and Table 7 (z/SO(3) generalization) report only single accuracy numbers with no variance or multiple seeds, despite ModelNet40 results typically being sensitive to initialization and rotation sampling.

The method restricts to classification via one-vs-rest binary heads; this is explicitly stated as a limitation and the extension to regression (very common in molecular/geometric learning, e.g., property prediction) is left to future work, substantially narrowing the claimed applicability of 'anisotropic geometric networks'.

The toy 'grid signal orientation' experiment is somewhat contrived (the task is seemingly designed exactly to require directional/basis selection the proposed method directly addresses), and the near-perfect 99.38% accuracy versus chance-level baselines, while illustrative, raises the question of whether the task is overly favorable to the proposed mechanism rather than representative of realistic settings.

The heavy formal apparatus (locally compact Hausdorff spaces, galaxies, quotient topologies, equicontinuity families) is used to establish results that are intuitively simple (max of an equicontinuous/Lipschitz family preserves Lipschitz continuity), and it is not clear this generality is necessary for the paper's actual applications (graphs and point clouds), making the theory section longer and more opaque than needed relative to its practical payoff.

No code or implementation release is mentioned, and several practical details (number of sampled candidates, number of refinement steps, choice of priors hd, regularization of per-class orientations) are given only qualitative/heuristic treatment in the appendix, raising reproducibility concerns for a method with many moving parts.

Comparisons to some baselines (e.g., CN-PointNet/CN-DGCNN, VN-PointNet/VN-DGCNN) are not clearly verified as faithfully reproduced versus taken from original papers under potentially different experimental protocols, and the margin of improvement over strong baselines (e.g., DGCNN 88.6 vs AC-DGCNN 91.7, VN-DGCNN 90.2 vs AC-DGCNN 91.7) is modest given the substantial added complexity and runtime cost of the proposed method.

strengths: Addresses a well-known and important open problem in equivariant ML (discontinuity of canonicalization maps) with a conceptually elegant solution: making canonicalization depend jointly on input and network via prior maximization.

Solid theoretical development: clear definitions of adaptive canonicalization, proofs of equicontinuity/continuity, and a universal approximation theorem (Thm. 13) showing the method exactly spans the space of continuous symmetry-preserving functions, which is a stronger and more satisfying result than typical canonicalization UATs.

The framework is instantiated concretely in two non-trivial, practically relevant settings (spectral GNN eigenbasis ambiguity and point-cloud rotation invariance), showing the theory is not merely abstract.

Broad and reasonably rigorous experimental evaluation across toy diagnostic tasks, TUDataset, large-scale OGB benchmarks, and ModelNet40 (including an out-of-distribution z/SO(3) rotation generalization test), consistently showing gains over equivariant architectures, augmentation, frame averaging, and standard/learned canonicalization baselines.
Useful ablations in the appendix (sampling vs. optimization-based prior maximization, node- vs graph-level anisotropic filters) that probe practical design choices and computational trade-offs.
Good engagement with related work, explicitly contrasting with Dym et al.'s impossibility result for continuous canonicalization and clarifying why adaptive canonicalization circumvents it.
weaknesses: The theory assumes exact maximization over the transformation group (argmax attained), but the practical implementation uses approximate sampling + local gradient refinement; the paper does not analyze how this approximation affects the proven continuity/invariance/UAT guarantees, leaving a gap between theoretical claims and what is actually deployed.

The acknowledged limitation that prior maximization requires D separate optimizations at inference/training time raises scalability concerns for problems with many classes (e.g., ogbg-molpcba with 128 classes); wall-clock/training-time overhead versus baselines is not reported, making the practical cost-benefit trade-off unclear.

Restriction to classification only (no regression) notably limits the scope of applicability, which is relevant since many geometric/molecular tasks are regression-based; this is deferred entirely to future work.

Some empirical gains, especially on larger OGB benchmarks, are modest relative to the reported standard deviations (e.g., ogbg-molhiv AUROC overlaps within ~1 std of PNA), raising questions about statistical significance of the improvements.

The toy grid-orientation task is constructed specifically to showcase the directional/anisotropic advantage of the proposed method (other methods are at literal chance level), which, while illustrative, is somewhat self-serving and should be weighted cautiously as evidence of general superiority.

Missing direct empirical comparison against some closely related, strong basis/sign-invariant spectral GNN baselines (e.g., Lim et al. 2022/2023, SpecFormer) that are discussed in related work but not included as competing methods in the main experiments.

The paper is dense and notation-heavy (galaxies, quotient spaces, functional calculus), which may hinder accessibility; combined with several architecture-specific design choices (band partitioning, truncation/padding of spectral coefficients) whose sensitivity is not thoroughly studied.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel theoretical framework (adaptive canonicalization / prior maximization) that provably yields continuous, symmetry-preserving, universally-approximating end-to-end models, addressing a well-known discontinuity problem in standard canonicalization (Dym et al. 2024) in a fundamentally different way than prior fixes (weighted frame averaging, energy-based canonicalization).

Rigorous and largely self-contained mathematical development: clear definitions (equicontinuity, adaptive canonicalization, prior maximization, symmetry-preserving prior maximization), with proofs establishing continuity (Thm 9) and that adaptively canonicalized functions exhaust the space of continuous symmetry-preserving functions (Thm 12), leading to a clean universal approximation theorem (Thm 13).

Thorough and honest positioning against closely related work (Kaba et al. 2023, Mondal et al. 2023, Shumaylov et al. 2025, Singhal et al. 2025, Dym et al. 2024, frame averaging), with detailed conceptual comparisons in the appendix rather than superficial citation.

Broad and consistent empirical validation: a diagnostic toy problem, TUDataset graph classification, large-scale OGB molecular/protein benchmarks, and ModelNet40 point cloud classification, with adaptive canonicalization outperforming equivariant architectures, augmentation, and standard canonicalization baselines across essentially all settings.

Extensive supplementary experiments (ablations on spectral band partitioning, GSO choice, backbone choice, sampling vs. optimization-based maximization, training stability, out-of-sample rotation generalization, sensitivity analysis, and an extension to point cloud segmentation and pretrained-model truncation canonicalization) that substantially strengthen confidence in the method's robustness and generality.

Practical algorithmic recipe (sample-and-refine random maximization) is provided along with a concentration-inequality-based justification for why finite-sample approximation of the prior maximum is reasonable.
weaknesses: The method requires solving D separate maximization problems (one per class) at both training and inference time; this is a nontrivial computational overhead that is only lightly benchmarked (mainly on small TUDataset graphs) and not clearly analyzed for settings with large D, e.g., ogbg-molpcba with 128 classes, raising scalability concerns that are acknowledged but not empirically resolved.

The toy 'grid signal orientation' experiment is constructed such that isotropic baselines are mathematically incapable of solving the task (remaining at chance level), which convincingly demonstrates the value of anisotropy but conflates the benefit of anisotropic filtering with the paper's central continuity/adaptive-canonicalization claim, making it a less clean test of the core theoretical contribution.

The extension to segmentation (App. G.10) uses an ad hoc entropy-based prior without any continuity guarantee, undercutting the paper's central theoretical selling point in a setting explicitly presented as a demonstration of broader applicability.

The framework is explicitly limited to classification-style settings (one-vs-rest with monotone priors); regression and other output structures are left as future work, which limits the immediate generality of the theoretical guarantees despite the framework being advertised as general.

In practice, the prior maximization is only approximately solved via sampling (and optional local refinement), so the continuity/universal-approximation guarantees hold rigorously only in an idealized limit; the gap between the theoretical guarantees and the practical, approximate implementation is acknowledged but not tightly characterized empirically (e.g., no direct measurement of how approximation quality affects continuity/stability at inference across domains).

Some ablations (e.g., spectral band partitioning, GSO comparison) are somewhat narrow in scope and specific to the A-NLSF instantiation, and broader comparisons (e.g., statistical significance testing, sensitivity to number of sampled transformations at scale) could strengthen the empirical claims further.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuine, well-known problem (discontinuity of canonicalization maps) with a reasonably rigorous theoretical treatment, including universal approximation guarantees for the resulting end-to-end models.

The framework generalizes beyond group-action symmetries to general 'transformation families' (e.g., image truncation), which is a nice conceptual broadening relative to prior canonicalization/frame-averaging work.

Extensive empirical validation across diverse domains: toy orientation task, TUDataset graph classification, large-scale OGB molecular/protein benchmarks, and ModelNet40 point cloud classification, with fairly comprehensive ablations in the appendix (sampling vs. optimization, GSO choice, band partitioning, backbone choice, sensitivity analysis, training stability, segmentation extension).
Clear and detailed positioning relative to closely related work (Kaba et al. 2023, Dym et al. 2024, Shumaylov et al. 2025, Singhal et al. 2025), with explicit discussion of conceptual differences.
Reasonably consistent empirical gains over equivariant architectures, data augmentation, and standard/learned canonicalization baselines across most benchmarks.
weaknesses: Prior maximization requires solving D separate optimization problems (one per class) at both train and inference time; this is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation but is not adequately addressed for high-class-count settings such as ogbg-molpcba (128 labels) or ModelNet40 (40 classes) — no runtime/memory comparison is reported for these experiments (only TUDataset has a compute table), leaving the practical scalability of the method largely unverified.

The theoretical continuity/universal-approximation guarantees rely on exact maximization over the transformation space, but in practice the method uses approximate sampling + a few gradient steps (Alg. 1); the paper only partially analyzes how this approximation affects the continuity guarantees (a generic concentration bound is sketched but not tied concretely to the architectures used), so the core theoretical selling point does not strictly transfer to the implemented system.

The core theoretical results (Thm. 6, 8, 9) rely on fairly elementary arguments (Lipschitz continuity of a max over an equicontinuous family), which, while useful for the application, represent limited independent theoretical novelty.

The illustrative toy 'grid signal orientation' experiment is constructed specifically so that isotropic spectral methods are at chance level while the proposed anisotropic method succeeds; this is somewhat of a designed-to-win benchmark and provides limited evidence of general-purpose superiority.

The framework as presented is restricted to classification (one-vs-rest) objectives; the proposed extension to segmentation via an entropy-based prior explicitly lacks the continuity guarantees that are the paper's central claimed contribution, undermining the generality of the theoretical story.

Several reported accuracy gains (e.g., point cloud results vs. VN-DGCNN/CN-DGCNN, ~1-1.5%) are modest relative to the added complexity and potential computational overhead of per-class rotation search, raising questions about the practical cost-benefit tradeoff.

No public code/repository is mentioned, and given the complexity of the method (galaxies, quotient spaces, band-wise unitary search, sample-and-refine optimization), reproducibility could be a concern despite detailed appendices.

OGB baselines, while reasonably strong, are somewhat dated relative to current state-of-the-art graph transformers/structured message passing methods, limiting the significance of the reported improvements.

strengths: Addresses a well-known and important open problem in equivariant ML: the discontinuity inherent to standard canonicalization (as proven impossible in general by Dym et al. 2024), by proposing a conceptually simple fix -- making canonicalization depend on the (co-trained) network output rather than only on the input.

The theoretical framework is rigorous and general: adaptive canonicalization is defined abstractly via equicontinuous families, prior maximization is shown to be a special case, and clean proofs establish continuity (Thm 9), exhaustiveness of symmetry-preserving continuous functions (Thm 12), and universal approximation (Thms 6, 13). The framework is not restricted to group-based symmetries, which broadens applicability (e.g., image truncation example).

Strong and broad empirical validation: toy orientation task, 5 TUDataset graph benchmarks, 3 large-scale OGB datasets, and ModelNet40 point cloud classification, with consistent improvements over equivariant architectures, augmentation, and multiple canonicalization baselines (OAP, CN, FA).

Extensive appendix content, including detailed comparison to related canonicalization/frame-averaging work, concentration bounds for the sampling-based approximation of prior maximization (via Cordonnier et al.'s volume-retaining analysis), many ablations (band partitioning, GSO choice, backbone choice, sampling vs. optimization), training stability diagnostics, and an extension to segmentation (ShapeNet), showing the idea is practically useful beyond the core setting.

Good illustrative motivation (mental rotation/cognitive psychology analogy) that makes the abstract construction intuitive, and a clear worked-out construction for two concrete architectures (spectral GNNs and point cloud networks) with full implementation detail in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Scalability concern acknowledged but not fully resolved: the method requires solving D separate maximizations (one per class) at both train and test time, which could be prohibitive for problems with many classes (e.g., ogbg-molpcba with 128 classes); the paper does not report wall-clock/memory costs for this dataset specifically, though it does report a general runtime comparison on smaller TUDataset instances.

There is a gap between the theoretical guarantees (exact maximization over U) and the practical implementation (finite random sampling plus a few gradient steps); while a concentration bound from prior work is invoked, it is not tailored/proven for this specific setting and the actual approximation error in experiments is not empirically quantified.

The extension to multi-class one-vs-rest and to segmentation (via an entropy-based prior) explicitly loses the continuity guarantee that is the paper's central theoretical selling point, which is honestly acknowledged but weakens the link between theory and the full set of reported experiments.

The framework assumes compactness/local compactness and equicontinuity conditions that, while satisfied in the given examples, require case-by-case verification; this could make it less of an "out of the box" tool than claimed for genuinely new, non-compact or less regular symmetry structures.

Some baseline comparisons (e.g., OAP+GIN, CN-PointNet/DGCNN) rely on numbers partly taken from prior papers or may not be as extensively hyperparameter-tuned as the proposed method, raising minor concerns about strict comparability of reported gains.

The paper is very notation-heavy and dense (galaxies, prior ensembles, symmetry preserving transformation families), which may hinder accessibility and adoption despite the appendix tutorial; a more compact main-text exposition with the core construction would improve clarity.
